disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through repeated exposure to aversive details. It is characterized by persistent re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of reminders, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month and causing functional impairment. The course can be acute or chronic, with onset sometimes delayed, and symptoms often fluctuating in intensity in response to triggers or life stressors. It is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement of a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of trauma-linked intrusions, avoidance, and hyperarousal.

narrative.stressor: Two and a half years ago, Georgina was working a late shift at the manufacturing plant when a long-time coworker and friend was caught in a malfunctioning press, suffering catastrophic injuries that she witnessed at close range before emergency services arrived. As one of the senior quality-control staff, she was pulled into the internal investigation, repeatedly reviewing incident footage and reports, and she quietly shouldered a sense that she "should have" noticed warning signs in the equipment she helped calibrate. Over the following months she began pulling back from extra shifts and community theater rehearsals, and friends noticed she had become unusually tense on the factory floor and increasingly reluctant to visit the plant after hours, but she attributed it to "just getting older" and work stress. The turning point came when the company installed a new line in the same area as the accident—Georgina started calling off shifts, skipping line-dancing and book club because she felt too on edge, and after a near-panic episode during a mandatory safety walk-through, her supervisor and a close friend from church urged her to see her primary care doctor, who referred her to psychiatry when it was clear that the work incident was still dominating her life more than two years later.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel constantly on edge at the plant and even around loud machines anywhere, like I can’t ever relax or let my guard down.”

narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Peter collapsed at home from a sudden cardiac arrhythmia and required emergency resuscitation; his wife found him unresponsive, and he later woke in the ICU with only fragments of what he’d been told was a very close brush with death. The episode disrupted his comfortable retirement routine of volunteering, painting, and walking with friends, and follow-up procedures and cardiac rehab kept him in and out of hospitals for months, surrounded by alarms and reminders of how suddenly life could end. As he tried to return to coordinating events at the senior center, he found himself quietly avoiding medical appointments, health-related conversations, and even certain routes on his walks that took him past the hospital, telling others he was just "tired of doctors" while gradually cutting back on activities that once grounded him. When his wife noticed that he would change the subject or leave the room whenever she or their children brought up his heart health or plans for future care—and that his world had shrunk to his garden and the TV over more than two years—she convinced him to mention it to his cardiologist, who recognized that his ongoing distress around the cardiac event warranted a mental health evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since my heart stopped, I go out of my way not to think or talk about what happened or anything to do with doctors.”

narrative.stressor: Just over two years ago, during a late evening commute home from her office, Katherine was riding a Metro-North train when it derailed after hitting a stalled vehicle at a crossing; several cars jackknifed, and she spent nearly an hour trapped among injured passengers before first responders could safely evacuate her. In the months that followed, she tried to throw herself back into work, hiking, and organizing her women-in-tech meetup, but her usual rail commute now involved passing the crash site and periodic service disruptions that brought the memories to the surface, and she began quietly rearranging meetings and social plans to avoid peak travel times or certain lines. As her company shifted to a hybrid schedule, she initially welcomed the flexibility but found herself increasingly constrained—turning down speaking invitations in the city, skipping off-Broadway shows with friends, and canceling weekend trips that required train travel—while colleagues noticed her once-energetic presence in cross-functional projects had dulled. After an embarrassing incident where she froze and left a team offsite early when a nearby train crossing alarm malfunctioned and caused a loud screech, her manager gently suggested employee assistance services; Katherine agreed after realizing that more than two years after the derailment, the way it still dominated her reactions and limited her life was no longer something she could "just power through."
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting these sudden, vivid memories of the train crash that pop into my head and completely derail whatever I’m doing.”
